title: The best Nooks alternatives in 2026
summary: Nooks alternatives for 2026, ranked. Artisan puts calling inside one AI outbound system, plus Orum, Salesfinity, Koncert and Kixie.
body_markdown:
The best Nooks alternative for most teams is Artisan, because it puts parallel dialing inside one AI-run outbound system rather than a standalone call floor. Artisan's pricing is usage-based and published, against Nooks' demo-gated quotes. Nooks is a capable pure parallel dialer. If calling is one channel in a wider motion, an all-in-one wins.


Nooks built a well-known virtual salesfloor: multi-line parallel dialing, AI answer detection, and live coaching that make it popular with high-volume calling teams. This focus is its strength and its boundary. Nooks dials; it does not source, email, or run the rest of your outbound. Teams that look for an alternative usually want the calling connected to everything else.

## How we chose


We weighted the criteria for a buyer who is deciding whether calling is a standalone need or one part of a motion:


1. How much of the outbound job the tool does. A pure dialer improves connect rates; a full system connects calling to sourcing, email, and reply-handling.


2. Pricing transparency. Published pricing beats demo-gated quotes, and we say so plainly.


3. Parallel-line depth and compliance. Line count, AI answer detection, and automatic enforcement of calling hours, do-not-call (DNC) rules, and consent-aware recording.


4. Deployment fit at scale. Pooled numbers, callback routing, CRM owner mapping, and reputation monitoring that protect a large team's connect rates.


## Why do teams look for a Nooks alternative?


Two reasons dominate: Nooks does only one channel, and its pricing is opaque.


Nooks is a calling product. It parallel dials, detects live answers, and runs a virtual salesfloor with coaching, and it does these things well. But it does not source leads, write or send email, or handle replies. So a team running real outbound pairs Nooks with a data tool, a sequencer, and a deliverability layer, then stitches them together and reconciles the reporting. The dialer is strong; the stack around it is the tax. See[Nooks vs. Aircall](https://www.artisan.co/blog/nooks-vs-aircall-which-should-you-choose-in-2026) .


On price, Nooks is demo-gated and billed annually. Third parties report figures around $4,000 to $5,000/user/year, but Nooks does not publish them. For a buyer trying to compare options without booking a sales call, this opacity is friction, and at the reported rates a large calling team is a serious annual line item. For a fuller breakdown, see[Nooks pricing and reviews](https://www.artisan.co/blog/nooks-pricing-and-reviews) .


We hear the same triggers again and again:


-


You are buying a dialer and a stack around it. The calling is one purchase; sourcing, email, and reply-handling are three more.


-


Pricing requires a demo. You cannot line Nooks up against alternatives on cost without a sales conversation.


-


Connect rates depend on number reputation. Managing spam flagging across a big team is ongoing work, and the category's top worry.


None of this makes Nooks a weak dialer. It simply puts the center of gravity in the wrong place for a team that wants calling to be one channel in an AI-run motion.


## The best Nooks alternatives in 2026


### 1. Artisan: Calling inside one AI-run outbound system


Artisan is the alternative for teams that want the dialer to be a step in a larger, AI-run motion rather than a standalone floor. Calls run as steps inside Ava's multichannel sequences alongside email and social media outreach, so the same system that sources a lead and writes the email also places the call and logs the outcome. Ava parallel dials up to three lines with AI answer detection, loads live AI talking points before the call connects, transcribes live, auto-classifies outcomes, drafts the follow-up email, and can drop a voicemail with automatic area-code matching.


The compliance and scale story is built for real teams, not only small and midsize businesses (SMBs). Numbers are pooled at the org level with personal callback routing, so a lead who calls back reaches the right rep's phone. Calling-hours enforcement, DNC checks, and consent-aware recording apply automatically per lead. Central admin maps CRM owners so calls log to the right rep, and per-number call ceilings plus carrier spam-reputation monitoring protect connect rates across a large team. Numbers are available in the US, Canada, the UK, Mexico, and Colombia.


The economics are the headline against Nooks. Artisan's pricing is usage-based: Ava's work runs on credits, so you pay for what she actually performs, whether that is qualifying, enriching, personalizing, or sending. You can try Ava for free, and you can read how the model works without booking a demo. The dialer sits inside that same system, with talking points, transcription, AI-drafted follow-ups, recordings, and analytics included in the motion rather than sold as a separate product.


The line count is a real limit. Artisan parallel dials up to 3 lines, while Orum reaches 5 to 10 and Nooks runs multi-line. A team whose entire motion is maximum-volume parallel calling, and nothing else, may still want a dedicated floor. For everyone whose calling sits inside a broader outbound motion, one system beats a dialer plus a stack. For a direct comparison, see[Artisan vs. Nooks](https://www.artisan.co/blog/artisan-vs-nooks) .


Chain of Events sourced over $700K of ARR in six months with Ava, a 20x return on its investment.


**Best for:** startups through enterprise that want calling as one channel in an AI-run outbound system.


**Who should pick something else:** pure call floors whose only job is maximum-volume parallel dialing at 5 to 10 lines.


**Pricing:** usage-based, with a free trial. See[artisan.co/pricing](https://www.artisan.co/pricing) .


### 2. Orum: Enterprise pure parallel


Orum is the alternative for large teams whose motion really is high-volume parallel calling and who need international reach. It parallel dials 5 to 10 lines with AI answer detection, offers international dialing on its Ascend tier, and acquired the conversation-intelligence tool Scout AI in July 2026. For a dedicated call floor at enterprise scale, Orum is an established option. See[Orum vs. Nooks](https://www.artisan.co/blog/orum-vs-nooks-which-should-you-choose-in-2026) .


The trade is the same as Nooks, sharpened. Orum is calling-only, and its live page is gated, with Launch reported around $250/user/month and Ascend custom-quoted. It is a pure dialer, so sourcing, email, and reply-handling live in other tools. Our[dialer roundup](https://www.artisan.co/blog/the-best-ai-dialers-and-parallel-dialers) compares the pure-parallel options in depth.


**Best for:** enterprise call floors that need 5 to 10 lines and broad international coverage.


**Who should pick something else:** teams that want calling connected to the rest of outbound, or published pricing.


**Pricing:** gated; Launch reported ~$250/user/month, up to 5 lines; Ascend custom, up to 10 lines.


### 3. Salesfinity: Transparent parallel pricing


Salesfinity is the pick for teams that want real parallel dialing without a demo to see the price. It publishes $149 to $349/user/month for five lines, which makes it the transparent alternative to Nooks and Orum in the pure-dialer tier. For a calling team that values knowing the cost up front, this openness is a genuine advantage.


Salesfinity is still a dedicated dialer, so the same boundary applies: it dials, and the rest of your outbound stack sits elsewhere. But among standalone parallel dialers, its pricing transparency stands out.


**Best for:** calling teams that want five-line parallel dialing at a published price.


**Who should pick something else:** teams that want the dialer inside a full outbound system.


**Pricing:** $149 to $349/user/month for five lines, per Salesfinity's pricing page.


### 4. Koncert: Multiple dialing modes


Koncert suits teams that want flexibility in how they dial. It offers several modes, an AI parallel dialer, a flow dialer, and an agent-assisted dialer, so reps can match a dialing style to each campaign. This range makes it adaptable across different calling motions within one tool.


Koncert is a dedicated dialing platform, so like the others in this tier it handles calls and not the surrounding motion. It publishes a per-seat ladder from $6 to $99/user/month depending on the mode, which helps buyers compare without a sales call.


**Best for:** teams that want to switch between parallel, flow, and agent-assisted dialing.


**Who should pick something else:** teams that want calling unified with sourcing, email, and replies.


**Pricing:** $6 to $99/user/month public ladder, per Koncert's pricing page.


### 5. Kixie: Dialer plus texting for SMB


Kixie is the alternative for smaller teams that want a power dialer bundled with texting and tight CRM integration. It pairs outbound calling with SMS and logs activity to your CRM, which suits SMB sales teams that live in one tool and want calls and texts in the same place. Its published per-seat pricing keeps it accessible.


Kixie is more power dialer than high-volume parallel floor, so it is a different shape from Nooks: lighter on parallel-line depth, broader on channel mix for a small team. It is a fit for SMB motions, not enterprise call floors. For more options, see[the best Kixie alternatives](https://www.artisan.co/blog/the-best-kixie-alternatives) .


**Best for:** SMB teams that want calling, texting, and CRM logging in one affordable tool.


**Who should pick something else:** teams that need high-line parallel dialing or an AI-run full outbound motion.


**Pricing:** published per-seat pricing, per Kixie's pricing page.


## Stay with Nooks if...


Nooks is the right call for a specific profile. Keep it if:


-


Your entire motion is maximum-volume parallel calling and you need five or more simultaneous lines with a full virtual salesfloor.


-


Live coaching and rep enablement on the call floor are central to how your team works.


-


You already run a settled stack for sourcing, email, and replies, and you only need a strong pure dialer to plug into it.


Switching away from a dedicated dialer to solve a problem it never had is a mistake. If your calling is truly standalone and you want a deep salesfloor, Nooks is a defensible place to stay. If calling is one channel among several, this is your signal to consolidate.


## How a standalone dialer compares to an AI BDR


The decision hinges on whether calling is your whole motion or one channel in it. A dedicated dialer like Nooks maximizes connect rates on the phone, and does nothing else. An[AI sales agent](https://www.artisan.co/ai-sales-agent) like Ava places calls as one step in a sequence that also sources a lead, writes and sends the email, and handles the reply, all in one system. For wider roundups, see[best autodialers](https://www.artisan.co/blog/best-autodialers) and[best outbound dialer](https://www.artisan.co/blog/best-outbound-dialer) .


If your team only calls, a pure dialer with more lines can win on raw parallel volume. If your team runs multichannel outbound, buying a standalone dialer means buying and stitching a stack around it. Consolidating into an[AI business development representative (BDR)](https://www.artisan.co/blog/ai-bdr) removes both the stitching and the demo-gated pricing. See also[Artisan vs. Aircall](https://www.artisan.co/blog/artisan-vs-aircall) and[the best CloudTalk alternatives](https://www.artisan.co/blog/the-best-cloudtalk-alternatives) .


## What changed in dialers in 2026?


-


Orum acquired the conversation-intelligence tool Scout AI in July 2026, deepening its post-call analytics.


-


Spam flagging and number reputation stayed the category's number-one buyer worry, pushing demand toward tools with automatic reputation monitoring and per-number ceilings.


-


Published dialer pricing gained ground against demo-gated enterprise quotes as buyers pushed back on quote-only models.


-


Parallel dialing moved from a standalone category toward a channel inside broader AI-run outbound systems.


## Frequently asked questions


**What is the best alternative to Nooks?** For teams that want calling connected to the rest of outbound, Artisan is the strongest alternative, because the dialer runs inside Ava's multichannel sequences. For a pure high-volume call floor, Orum is the closest dedicated rival, with 5 to 10 parallel lines.


**What is the best enterprise alternative to Nooks?** Artisan is the pick for teams that want calling governed inside one system: pooled org-level numbers, callback routing, automatic DNC and calling-hours enforcement, CRM owner mapping, and reputation monitoring. Orum is the enterprise choice if the motion is purely maximum-volume parallel calling.


**How much does Nooks cost?** Nooks does not publish pricing; third parties report roughly $4,000 to $5,000/user/year, annual and demo-gated. Artisan works differently: its pricing is usage-based, so you pay for the work Ava performs rather than for a fixed seat bundle, and you can try her for free.


**How many parallel lines does Artisan support?** Artisan parallel dials up to 3 lines with AI answer detection. Orum reaches 5 to 10 lines and Nooks runs multi-line. For a team whose whole motion is maximum-volume calling, this line-count difference matters; for teams where calling is one channel in a broader sequence, 3 lines inside one system is usually the better trade.


**Does Artisan replace a full dialer for calling teams?** For teams that run multichannel outbound, yes: the dialer is a native step in Ava's sequences with talking points, transcription, and auto-classified outcomes. For teams whose only motion is high-line parallel calling, a dedicated high-line floor like Nooks or Orum can still make sense.


**Is Salesfinity cheaper than Nooks?** Salesfinity publishes $149 to $349/user/month for five lines, while Nooks is demo-gated, so a direct comparison requires a Nooks quote. Both are dedicated dialers sold per seat, whereas Artisan charges for usage, though Artisan tops out at three parallel lines rather than five.
